NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The intervention is a modified pipe lining material that releases a nitrification-inhibiting compound slowly into the bulk water phase. Standard practice uses cement-mortar or epoxy linings that are passive barriers against corrosion but do not actively inhibit microbial processes. This mitigation departs by incorporating a bioactive compound that specifically targets the enzymatic pathway of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria without affecting disinfectant residual. The closest existing practice is copper pipe usage which has some biostatic properties but relies on ionic release rather than targeted enzymatic inhibition and is not applicable to large-diameter mains. The mechanism works by the lining material slowly releasing a compound that irreversibly inhibits ammonia monooxygenase, the key enzyme in nitrification, thereby breaking the biofilm's metabolic pathway.

PHYSICS CHECK
The governing physical relation is the Monod kinetics for nitrification: μ = μ_max × [S]/(K_s + [S]), where μ is the growth rate, μ_max is the maximum growth rate, [S] is the substrate concentration (ammonia), and K_s is the half-saturation constant. The intervention reduces μ_max by inhibiting the enzyme responsible for ammonia oxidation. With a 90% inhibition of ammonia monooxygenase activity, the nitrification rate would drop by at least 85% based on enzyme kinetics, reducing nitrite production to below regulatory levels while maintaining chlorine residual above 1.0 mg/L.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Components, materials, instruments, procedure for INSTALLING and RUNNING the intervention:

Standard Practice Bill:
- Cement-mortar lining material
- Standard pipe installation equipment
- Routine disinfection procedure with chlorine
- Water quality monitoring for chlorine residual

Intervention Bill:
- Modified epoxy lining material with encapsulated nitrification inhibitor (procured standard epoxy with added bioactive compound)
- Standard pipe installation equipment (no change)
- Modified disinfection procedure with initial higher chlorine dose to activate inhibitor release (within standard chlorine handling protocols)
- Water quality monitoring for chlorine residual and nitrite (existing monitoring capabilities)

Note: The encapsulated nitrification inhibitor would need to be developed but would be formulated as a standard additive to existing epoxy lining materials, requiring no new equipment or major process changes.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Lining material: Modified epoxy with encapsulated inhibitor vs standard epoxy (slight increase in material cost, but within same procurement category)
- Installation equipment: No change (same burden)
- Disinfection procedure: Initial higher chlorine dose (temporary, within standard chlorine handling protocols - same burden class)
- Monitoring: Addition of nitrite testing (existing capability, minimal additional cost - same burden class)

Conclusion: Same burden class. The intervention uses existing infrastructure and standard materials with minor modifications, resulting in no increase in burden class compared to standard practice.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Install the modified lining in a representative dead-end main section with known nitrification issues. Monitor chlorine residual and nitrite levels at the farthest customer point for 90 days during summer demand conditions (25°C). Compare with a control section with standard lining.

Instruments: Chlorine residual analyzer, nitrite ion-selective electrode, flow meters, temperature sensors.

Pass/Fail Threshold: The intervention is successful if nitrite levels remain below 0.1 mg/L (typical regulatory limit) while maintaining chlorine residual above 1.0 mg/L at all times. The control section should experience at least three nitrification episodes (nitrite > 0.1 mg/L) during the same period.

Duration: 90 days of continuous monitoring.

Kill Criterion: If nitrite levels exceed 0.1 mg/L at any point during the test period, or if chlorine residual drops below 1.0 mg/L for more than 4 consecutive hours, the intervention is considered ineffective and must be re-evaluated.
